title: Urine Clues That Need a Second Test: Sterile Pyuria, Darkening Urine and Non-Glucose Reducing Sugar
summary: Learn when sterile pyuria should prompt mycobacterial cultures, why urine that blackens on standing points to homogentisic acid or melanin, and how to act on a newborn’s urine that reduces copper but is negative for glucose oxidase.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 29 Hits 13, 14 and 15. Checked against Glen 2016 (read via a page-fetch tool; Europe PMC full text empty), Simerville 2005 (AAFP page, read via a page-fetch tool), Bilsen 2023, Kapoor 2008, Mantica 2021, Zatkova 2020, Milella 2024, Mishe’el 2016, Sacks 2011, Coelho 2017, Badiu Tișa 2022, Succoio 2022 and Welling 2017. Where the sources qualify the reviewer the lesson teaches the source: sterile pyuria has many ordinary causes and renal tuberculosis is considered when it persists, especially with risk factors; the reducing-substance screen is neither sensitive nor specific, and galactosaemia is confirmed by GALT activity or gene analysis while the diet is changed at once. Not taught (not found in the sources read): that the urine in renal tuberculosis is acidic.

objectives: Define sterile pyuria, list common causes, and state when and how to test urine for tuberculosis.
Explain why urine darkens on standing in alkaptonuria and in disseminated melanoma.
Interpret a positive copper-reduction test with a negative glucose-oxidase strip in a newborn, and state the guideline actions for suspected galactosaemia.

scenes.title: Three clues, three second tests
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three urine specimens whose routine results leave a question. (1) An adult with months of pyuria and microscopic haematuria; routine bacterial cultures are repeatedly negative. (2) An adult’s urine that looked ordinary when voided but turned black after standing in the cup. (3) A 7-day-old with vomiting and jaundice: copper-reduction test for reducing substances positive, glucose-oxidase strip negative. Question token: “Which second test does each clue call for?”

cues.text: Three urine specimens leave a question. An adult with months of white cells and microscopic blood in the urine, but every routine culture is negative.
An adult’s urine that looked ordinary when passed but turned black while standing. And a seven-day-old whose urine reduces copper but leaves the glucose strip negative.
Which second test does each clue call for?

props.label: Which second test does each clue call for?

scenes.title: What the routine tests can and cannot see
scenes.altText: Schematic cards. Pyuria card (Bilsen 2023): pyuria means white cells in urine; commonly accepted cutoffs for significant pyuria are 10 leukocytes/µL or 5–10 per high-power field, and they depend on the counting method. Culture card (Mantica 2021; Kapoor 2008): routine urine culture targets ordinary bacteria; Mycobacterium tuberculosis needs acid-fast smear and dedicated mycobacterial culture, which takes weeks. Sugar card (Sacks 2011): strip glucose pads use the glucose oxidase reaction, specific for glucose; reducing-substance (copper-reduction) methods also react with non-glucose sugars and many drugs. Colour card (Simerville 2005): melanin, bile pigments and methaemoglobin are listed pathological causes of brownish-black urine.

cues.text: Start with what routine tests see. Pyuria means white cells in the urine. Common cutoffs are ten per microlitre or five to ten per high-power field, and they depend on how the cells are counted.
A routine urine culture looks for ordinary bacteria. Tuberculosis needs an acid-fast smear and a dedicated mycobacterial culture that takes weeks.
The strip’s glucose pad uses glucose oxidase, a reaction specific for glucose. A copper-reduction test for reducing substances also reacts with other sugars, and with many drugs.
And colour: melanin, bile pigments and methaemoglobin are listed causes of brownish-black urine.

scenes.title: Sterile pyuria and urine that darkens
scenes.altText: Sterile pyuria card (Glen 2016): no agreed definition, typically > 5–8 leucocytes/hpf with negative cultures; causes include a recently treated UTI, Chlamydia, prostatitis, stones, tumours, catheters, drug-induced interstitial nephritis and pregnancy; consider renal tuberculosis in chronic sterile pyuria, especially with residence in an endemic region, immunosuppression or weight loss. Tuberculosis card (Kapoor 2008; Mantica 2021): sterile pyuria is the classic urine finding; microscopic haematuria in up to 50%, gross haematuria in about 10%; send at least three consecutive early-morning first-void samples for AFB culture (some sources say five); smear about 20% sensitive; culture is the gold standard, liquid culture positive in at least 9–10 days and negative only at 6 weeks. Darkening card (Zatkova 2020; Milella 2024): alkaptonuria is an autosomal recessive deficiency of homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase in tyrosine metabolism; homogentisic acid is excreted in urine, which darkens on standing, on exposure to oxygen or alkali, from birth; ochronosis and arthropathy usually appear from about age 30. Melanuria card (Mishe’el 2016): black urine is an uncommon finding in disseminated melanoma; in the case report, dark yellow urine turned black after exposure to air.

cues.text: Sterile pyuria means white cells with negative cultures; one practical guide says typically more than five to eight per high-power field. The common causes are ordinary: a recently treated infection, Chlamydia, stones, catheters, drugs, pregnancy.

Renal tuberculosis belongs on the list when sterile pyuria persists, especially with risk factors. Send at least three early-morning urines for acid-fast culture: the smear catches only about one case in five.

Now the urine that darkens. In alkaptonuria, homogentisate dioxygenase is missing, so homogentisic acid spills into the urine and darkens on standing, with air or with alkali, from birth. Joint and cartilage pigment usually appear from about age thirty.
Melanin is the other dark pigment. In disseminated melanoma the urine can turn black after exposure to air. It is uncommon.

scenes.title: The neonate whose urine reduces copper
scenes.altText: Screen card (Coelho 2017; Badiu Tișa 2022; Succoio 2022): urine reducing substances can point to galactosaemia but the test is neither sensitive nor specific — false positives with fructosuria, lactosuria, severe liver disease, antibiotic treatment, prematurity or renal tubular acidosis; false negatives when the infant is on intravenous feeding. Galactose metabolites (galactose-1-phosphate, galactitol) are more specific. Confirmation card (Welling 2017 guideline): confirm classical galactosaemia by red-cell GALT activity and/or GALT gene analysis; start a galactose-restricted diet immediately when it is suspected, without waiting for confirmation. Hook answers card.

cues.text: Copper reduction positive and glucose oxidase negative means a reducing substance that is not glucose. In a sick newborn on milk, galactose is the worry.
But the screen is neither sensitive nor specific. Fructose, lactose, liver disease and antibiotics can make it positive; an infant on intravenous feeding can be falsely negative.

Confirm with red-cell GALT enzyme activity or GALT gene analysis. The international guideline says to start a galactose-restricted diet as soon as galactosaemia is suspected, without waiting for the result.

Hook answers: early-morning acid-fast cultures for persistent sterile pyuria; a homogentisic acid or melanin workup for the urine that blackened; and for the newborn, diet change now and GALT confirmation.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Sterile pyuria with haematuria = renal tuberculosis” (✓ most sterile pyuria has ordinary causes; tuberculosis is considered when it persists, especially with risk factors); “A negative AFB smear rules out urinary tuberculosis” (✓ smear about 20% sensitive; send at least three early-morning cultures); “Reducing substances positive = galactosaemia confirmed” (✓ screen is non-specific; confirm with GALT activity or gene, but start the diet now).

cues.text: Trap one: sterile pyuria with blood means renal tuberculosis. No: most sterile pyuria has ordinary causes. Tuberculosis is the one you must not miss when it persists.
Trap two: a negative acid-fast smear rules out urinary tuberculosis. No: the smear catches only about one in five; culture three early-morning samples.
Trap three: reducing substances confirm galactosaemia. No: the screen is non-specific. Confirm with GALT testing, but change the diet now.

props.title: ✗ “Sterile pyuria + blood = renal TB.”
lines: ✓ Usually ordinary causes; TB if persistent

props.title: ✗ “Reducing sugar + = galactosaemia.”

scenes.title: Sterile, Standing, Sugar
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Sterile, Standing, Sugar.” STERILE pyuria that persists → slow mycobacterial culture on three early-morning urines. STANDING urine that turns black → homogentisic acid or melanin. SUGAR that reduces copper but is not glucose → think galactose, start the diet, confirm GALT. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: Sterile, Standing, Sugar. Persistent sterile pyuria: slow acid-fast cultures. Urine that blackens on standing: homogentisic acid or melanin. Sugar that reduces copper but is not glucose: think galactose.
Where it breaks: most sterile pyuria is not tuberculosis; other pigments also make urine brown or black; and the reducing-substance screen has false positives and false negatives.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Persistent sterile pyuria → ≥3 early-morning AFB cultures · black on standing → homogentisic acid or melanin”, “Copper + / glucose oxidase − in a newborn → galactose-restricted diet now, confirm GALT”.

cues.text: When a routine urinalysis leaves a clue unexplained, order the second test it points to: early-morning mycobacterial cultures for persistent sterile pyuria, a homogentisic acid or melanin workup for urine that blackens on standing, and GALT confirmation, with a galactose-restricted diet started at once, for a newborn whose urine reduces copper but not glucose oxidase.

explanation.what: Plain language: some urine results are clues rather than answers. White cells without a growing organism may mean a germ the routine culture cannot grow, such as tuberculosis, though most cases have ordinary causes. Urine that turns black after it stands contains a pigment that forms in air, from homogentisic acid or melanin. And a sugar test that reacts while the glucose test stays negative means a sugar other than glucose, which in a sick newborn raises galactosaemia. Scientific terms: pyuria, sterile pyuria, acid-fast bacilli (AFB), mycobacterial culture, genitourinary tuberculosis, alkaptonuria, homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase (HGD), homogentisic acid (HGA), ochronosis, melanuria, glucose oxidase, copper reduction, reducing substances, classical galactosaemia, galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase (GALT), galactose-1-phosphate, galactitol.
explanation.why: Routine culture is set up for ordinary bacteria, so slow-growing mycobacteria are missed unless asked for. Homogentisic acid and melanin precursors oxidise to dark pigments on standing. Glucose oxidase reacts only with glucose, whereas copper reduction detects any reducing substance, so the pair separates glucose from other sugars.
explanation.measure: Pyuria cutoffs commonly 10 leukocytes/µL or 5–10/hpf (method-dependent); sterile pyuria typically > 5–8 leucocytes/hpf with negative cultures (no agreed definition). Urinary tuberculosis: at least three consecutive early-morning first-void samples for AFB culture (some sources say five); smear about 20% sensitive; culture 80–90% sensitive; liquid culture positive in ≥ 9–10 days, negative at 6 weeks; microscopic haematuria in up to 50%. Galactosaemia: confirm by red-cell GALT activity and/or GALT gene analysis; galactose-restricted diet started immediately on suspicion.
explanation.differs: Sterile pyuria from ordinary causes vs renal tuberculosis (persistent, risk factors); alkaptonuria (homogentisic acid, from birth, later ochronosis) vs melanuria (disseminated melanoma); glucose oxidase (glucose only) vs copper reduction (any reducing substance); reducing-substance screen vs GALT confirmation.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: choose the specimen for urinary tuberculosis, name the substance that darkens alkaptonuric urine, or pick the next step for a newborn with copper-reduction positive, glucose-oxidase negative urine.

comparisons.title: Glucose oxidase vs copper reduction

right.label: Copper reduction
points: Interference from drugs and other sugars

comparisons.distinguisher: Positive copper reduction with negative glucose oxidase means a reducing substance that is not glucose.

comparisons.title: Alkaptonuria vs melanuria
comparisons.distinguisher: An inherited metabolic block from birth vs a pigment shed by widespread melanoma.

mnemonic.text: Sterile, Standing, Sugar: persistent STERILE pyuria → slow acid-fast cultures; urine that blackens on STANDING → homogentisic acid or melanin; a SUGAR that reduces copper but is not glucose → think galactose, change the diet and confirm GALT.
mnemonic.explanation: Three routine findings, each pointing to a specific second test.
mnemonic.limitation: Most sterile pyuria is not tuberculosis; other pigments (bile pigments, methaemoglobin) also give brown-black urine; the reducing-substance screen has false positives and false negatives.

takeaway: When a routine urinalysis leaves a clue unexplained, order the second test it points to: early-morning mycobacterial cultures for persistent sterile pyuria, a homogentisic acid or melanin workup for urine that blackens on standing, and GALT confirmation, with a galactose-restricted diet started at once, for a newborn whose urine reduces copper but not glucose oxidase.

questions.stem: An adult has had pyuria and microscopic haematuria for several months. Routine bacterial urine cultures are repeatedly negative, and the patient grew up in a region where tuberculosis is common. Which specimen plan best tests for urinary tuberculosis?

options.text: At least three consecutive early-morning urine samples for acid-fast culture
options.rationale: Correct. Reviews recommend at least three consecutive early-morning, first-void samples for mycobacterial culture, the gold standard.

options.text: One random urine for an acid-fast smear only
options.rationale: Incorrect. The urine smear is only about 20% sensitive, so a single negative smear does not rule out tuberculosis.

options.text: Repeat routine bacterial culture until it turns positive
options.rationale: Incorrect. Routine culture targets ordinary bacteria; mycobacteria need dedicated culture.

options.text: No further testing, because sterile pyuria is never significant
options.rationale: Incorrect. Persistent sterile pyuria with risk factors is a reason to consider renal tuberculosis.

questions.stem: A 7-day-old with vomiting and jaundice has urine that is positive by copper reduction but negative on the glucose-oxidase strip. What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Suspect galactosaemia: start a galactose-restricted diet and confirm with GALT activity or gene analysis
options.rationale: Correct. The pair means a reducing substance that is not glucose; the guideline says to change the diet at once and confirm with GALT testing.
Incorrect. Glucose oxidase is specific for glucose, and it is negative.

options.text: Keep feeding milk until the GALT result returns
options.rationale: Incorrect. The guideline says not to wait for confirmation before restricting galactose.

options.text: Treat the positive reducing test as diagnostic and skip confirmation
options.rationale: Incorrect. The screen is neither sensitive nor specific (fructose, lactose, liver disease and antibiotics can make it positive), so confirmation is still needed.

questions.stem: Urine from an adult with early-onset arthritis and dark pigment in the ear cartilage looks ordinary when voided but darkens on standing. Which substance is most likely responsible?

options.text: Homogentisic acid, from deficiency of homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase
options.rationale: Correct. In alkaptonuria homogentisic acid is excreted in urine and darkens on standing; ochronotic pigment in cartilage and joints appears later in life.
Incorrect. Melanuria also darkens in air, but it is uncommon and does not explain ochronosis of cartilage and joints.
Incorrect. Galactose is a newborn reducing-substance clue; darkening on standing together with cartilage and joint pigment is the pattern of homogentisic acid.
Incorrect. Darkening on standing together with cartilage and joint pigment is the pattern of homogentisic acid, not of haemolysis.

references.citation: Glen P, Prashar A, Hawary A. Sterile pyuria: a practical management guide. Br J Gen Pract. 2016;66(644):e225-e227. doi:10.3399/bjgp16x684217
references.usedFor: Read via a page-fetch tool (Europe PMC full text empty). No agreed definition of sterile pyuria; typically > 5–8 leucocytes/hpf with negative cultures; infectious and non-infectious causes (recently treated UTI, Chlamydia, prostatitis, stones, neoplasms, catheters, drug-induced interstitial nephritis, pregnancy); renal tuberculosis considered in chronic sterile pyuria, especially in endemic-region patients, the immunocompromised or those with weight loss; three consecutive first-void morning samples for AFB and PCR.

references.citation: Simerville JA, Maxted WC, Pahira JJ. Urinalysis: a comprehensive review. Am Fam Physician. 2005;71(6):1153-1162.
references.usedFor: Read via a page-fetch tool. Tuberculosis among causes of sterile pyuria; Table 1: melanin, bile pigments and methaemoglobin as pathological causes of brownish-black urine.

references.citation: Bilsen MP, Aantjes MJ, van Andel E, et al. Current Pyuria Cutoffs Promote Inappropriate Urinary Tract Infection Diagnosis in Older Women. Clin Infect Dis. 2023;76(12):2070-2076. doi:10.1093/cid/ciad099
references.usedFor: Commonly accepted pyuria cutoffs of 10 leukocytes/µL and 5–10 leukocytes/hpf; cutoffs vary and depend on quantification method.

references.citation: Kapoor R, Ansari MS, Mandhani A, Gulia A. Clinical presentation and diagnostic approach in cases of genitourinary tuberculosis. Indian J Urol. 2008;24(3):401-405. doi:10.4103/0970-1591.42626
references.usedFor: Sterile pyuria is the classic urine finding of genitourinary tuberculosis, with or without haematuria; gross haematuria in about 10%, microscopic in up to 50%; preferably five consecutive early-morning specimens; urine culture needs special media and 6–8 weeks.

references.citation: Mantica G, Ambrosini F, Riccardi N, et al. Genitourinary Tuberculosis: A Comprehensive Review of a Neglected Manifestation in Low-Endemic Countries. Antibiotics (Basel). 2021;10(11):1399. doi:10.3390/antibiotics10111399
references.usedFor: “Sterile” pyuria and/or haematuria may be the first findings; urine AFB smear about 97% specific but about 20% sensitive; at least three early-morning first-void midstream samples on consecutive days for AFB culture; culture gold standard (80–90% sensitive); liquid culture at least 9–10 days to positive, 6 weeks to negative.

references.citation: Zatkova A, Ranganath L, Kadasi L. Alkaptonuria: Current Perspectives. Appl Clin Genet. 2020;13:37-47. doi:10.2147/tacg.s186773
references.usedFor: Alkaptonuria is an autosomal recessive deficiency of homogentisate dioxygenase in tyrosine metabolism with accumulation of homogentisic acid; homogentisic aciduria from birth, with urine darkening on standing; ochronosis and osteoarthropathy usually from around age 30.

references.citation: Milella MS, Geminiani M, Trezza A, et al. Alkaptonuria: From Molecular Insights to a Dedicated Digital Platform. Cells. 2024;13(12):1072. doi:10.3390/cells13121072
references.usedFor: Homogentisic acid auto-oxidises and polymerises to a dark pigment; alkaptonuric urine darkens on exposure to oxygen or alkali; circulating homogentisic acid is largely excreted in urine.

references.citation: Mishe’el S, Ziv M, Bisharat N. Black Urine and Black Pleural Fluid: A Distinctive Presentation of Metastatic Melanoma. Eur J Case Rep Intern Med. 2016;3(4):000416. doi:10.12890/2016_000416
references.usedFor: Case report: black urine (melanuria) is an uncommon finding in disseminated melanoma; the urine was dark yellow and turned black after exposure to air; Fontana-positive pigment showed melanin; alkaptonuria was among the causes of dark urine considered.

references.citation: Sacks DB, Arnold M, Bakris GL, et al. Guidelines and recommendations for laboratory analysis in the diagnosis and management of diabetes mellitus. Diabetes Care. 2011;34(6):e61-e99. doi:10.2337/dc11-9998
references.usedFor: Urine glucose section: strip methods with reactions specific for glucose are recommended and commercial strips use the glucose oxidase reaction; reducing-substance methods are not recommended because of interference from numerous drugs and non-glucose sugars.

references.citation: Coelho AI, Rubio-Gozalbo ME, Vicente JB, Rivera I. Sweet and sour: an update on classic galactosemia. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2017;40(3):325-342. doi:10.1007/s10545-017-0029-3
references.usedFor: Urine reducing-substance screening can be informative but is not sensitive or specific: false positives from fructosuria, lactosuria, severe liver disease or antibiotic treatment; false negatives on intravenous feeding; galactose metabolites (Gal-1-P, galactitol) more specific.

references.citation: Badiu Tișa I, Achim AC, Cozma-Petruț A. The Importance of Neonatal Screening for Galactosemia. Nutrients. 2022;15(1):10. doi:10.3390/nu15010010
references.usedFor: Reducing substances in urine while the infant takes breast milk or lactose formula as an initial diagnostic clue; the test lacks sensitivity and specificity (same false positives and false negatives as Coelho 2017).

references.citation: Succoio M, Sacchettini R, Rossi A, Parenti G, Ruoppolo M. Galactosemia: Biochemistry, Molecular Genetics, Newborn Screening, and Treatment. Biomolecules. 2022;12(7):968. doi:10.3390/biom12070968
references.usedFor: Urine reducing substances can point to galactosaemia but are also positive in prematurity, renal tubular acidosis, some drugs and other metabolic diseases.

references.citation: Welling L, Bernstein LE, Berry GT, et al. International clinical guideline for the management of classical galactosemia: diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2017;40(2):171-176. doi:10.1007/s10545-016-9990-5
references.usedFor: Recommendation 1: confirm classical galactosaemia by red-cell GALT activity and/or GALT gene analysis; Recommendation 4: start a galactose-restricted diet immediately when classical galactosaemia is suspected, without waiting for confirmation.

claims.text: Common pyuria cutoffs (10 leukocytes/µL or 5–10/hpf) and their method dependence.
Sterile pyuria definition (no agreed definition; typically > 5–8/hpf with negative cultures), ordinary causes, and when to consider renal tuberculosis.
Genitourinary tuberculosis urine findings (sterile pyuria, haematuria frequency) and AFB testing (≥ 3 early-morning samples, smear ~20% sensitive, culture gold standard and turnaround).
Alkaptonuria: autosomal recessive HGD deficiency, homogentisic acid in urine darkening on standing, with oxygen or alkali, from birth; ochronosis from about age 30.
Melanuria: uncommon in disseminated melanoma; urine turning black after air exposure; melanin among causes of brownish-black urine.
Glucose oxidase strip reaction is specific for glucose; reducing-substance methods also react with non-glucose sugars and drugs.
Urine reducing-substance screen for galactosaemia: informative but neither sensitive nor specific; listed false positives and false negatives.
Confirm by red-cell GALT activity and/or gene analysis; start a galactose-restricted diet immediately on suspicion.
Reviewer’s “in acidic urine” as a clue to renal tuberculosis.
claims.note: Not found in the sources read (Glen 2016, Kapoor 2008, Mantica 2021, Simerville 2005); not taught.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 29 Hit 13 says sterile pyuria with haematuria in acidic urine should make you think of renal tuberculosis. Glen 2016 and Simerville 2005 list many commoner causes of sterile pyuria (recently treated UTI, Chlamydia, stones, catheters, drugs, pregnancy) and advise considering tuberculosis in chronic sterile pyuria, especially with risk factors; acidic urine as a clue was not found in any source read. The lesson teaches the differential and the AFB culture plan and does not teach the pH clue (register flag rv-sterile-pyuria-acid-urine-tb).

Ch. 29 Hit 15 presents reducing-sugar positive, glucose-oxidase negative urine in a neonate as the galactosaemia clue. Coelho 2017 and Badiu Tișa 2022 say the urine reducing-substance screen is neither sensitive nor specific (false positives with fructosuria, lactosuria, liver disease, antibiotics; false negatives on intravenous feeding), and the Welling 2017 guideline confirms by GALT activity or gene analysis while starting a galactose-restricted diet at once (register flag rv-reducing-substance-galactosemia).
